headline: Shopper bags RTX 5080 for $702 at Walmart, saving almost $800 off current retail.
summary: A lucky shopper found a PNY RTX 5080 for $702.56 at Walmart, a massive discount of over $546 from its listed price and less than half of what it sells for at other major retailers.
details: A lucky shopper scored a PNY-branded Nvidia RTX 5080 for just $702.56 at Walmart. This was a discount of $546.44 from its listed price of $1,249, and significantly below Nvidia's suggested retail price of $999.

The same PNY RTX 5080 OC graphics card is currently listed at over $1,500 on Amazon, Newegg, and Best Buy. This makes the Walmart clearance price less than half of what the GPU currently costs at major retailers.

The PNY GeForce RTX 5080 OC is a factory-overclocked version designed for 4K gaming and content creation. It features 10,752 CUDA cores, 16GB of GDDR7 memory on a 256-bit bus, and a boost clock of 2.73 GHz.

Walmart's clearance aisles have previously offered similar GPU bargains, including another RTX 5080 for $562.49 and an RTX 5060 Ti for $80. These deals highlight the potential for significant savings for vigilant shoppers.

While such deals offer incredible value, they carry inherent risks. Items could be customer returns, have damaged packaging, or even be swapped units, making careful inspection crucial before completing the purchase.

headline_marked: [[Modder attaches CPU cooler to GTX 1080 Ti]], drops temps by 32°C, gains 9% FPS and 30W savings
headline: Modder attaches CPU cooler to GTX 1080 Ti, drops temps by 32°C, gains 9% FPS and 30W savings
summary: An enthusiast's custom GPU cooling solution for the GTX 1080 Ti achieved a massive 32°C temperature reduction, 30W power savings, and 9% higher FPS. This unconventional mod significantly boosts performance and efficiency.
details: TrashBench successfully modded an Nvidia GTX 1080 Ti, 1070, and 1060 by replacing their stock coolers with a dual-tower CPU cooler. This unconventional approach led to significant improvements, including higher FPS, increased clock speeds, lower temperatures, and reduced power consumption. The GTX 1080 Ti saw up to a 32°C temperature drop.

The modification involved grinding parts of the stock cooler's finstack to expose the metal plate touching the GPU core. This allowed for a CPU cooler to be directly mounted onto the GPU die, bypassing the original cooling solution.

Initial tests on a GTX 1060 with a single-tower CPU cooler resulted in the card running 9°C cooler than its stock configuration, alongside slightly improved clock speeds. This proved the viability of the concept.
Further refinement with a dual-tower CPU cooler on the GTX 1060 led to a 6°C temperature reduction and a 9% increase in FPS in "Shadow of the Tomb Raider" compared to the stock cooler.
The GTX 1070 saw even more dramatic results, running a full 20°C cooler and consuming 15W less power. It also achieved 7% more FPS in-game with a stable overclock of 2,177 MHz.
For the high-power GTX 1080 Ti (250W TDP), TrashBench first established a baseline using a transplanted stock 1060 cooler, which ran 8°C hotter under load.

Against this baseline, the dual-tower CPU cooler on the GTX 1080 Ti achieved the same clocks while consuming 30W less power, a 12% reduction. It also ran up to 30°C cooler than the stock setup, with a sustained 19°C drop even after overclocking.
These results demonstrate the potential for extreme cooling solutions in custom PC builds. TrashBench has a history of similar projects, previously modding a GTX 960 and an RTX 3080 with server AIOs.
